turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (PATIENT): I have not had falls. I slid down, there's a difference, and I'm tired, so can we just get on with it.
[SEG0002] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Doctor, thanks for squeezing us in. Mum's had two falls over the past few weeks, and she's dizzy whenever she gets up.
[SEG0003] person_3 (DOCTOR): Alright. Joan, when you say you slid, what actually happened?
[SEG0004] person_1 (PATIENT): Um, my knees went soft and I ended up on the lino. Twice. I didn't trip over anything.
[SEG0005] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Once in the hallway on Tuesday night, and once in the kitchen about three weeks back. She went down hard the first time. I heard it from the lounge.
[SEG0006] person_1 (PATIENT): Three weeks? No. It was this week, Tuesday and then yesterday morning. And I didn't go down hard.
[SEG0007] person_3 (DOCTOR): Did you black out at all, or did you know you were going down?
[SEG0008] person_1 (PATIENT): I knew the whole time. No blackout.
[SEG0009] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): She didn't lose consciousness. She went white and grabbed the bench, though.
[SEG0010] person_3 (DOCTOR): Any chest pain with these episodes? Or the heart racing?
[SEG0011] person_1 (PATIENT): No chest pain. Heart's fine. I'm just worn out.
[SEG0012] person_3 (DOCTOR): Did you hit your head, vomit, or go weak down one side?
[SEG0013] person_1 (PATIENT): No. None of that. Can we not do the whole catalogue.
[SEG0014] person_3 (DOCTOR): The dizziness, is it mainly when you stand?
[SEG0015] person_1 (PATIENT): Only if I get up quick. A bit swimmy for a few seconds, then it's gone. Not all day.
[SEG0016] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): It's every time she stands, especially in the morning. She has to hold the bench. She's watering it down.
[SEG0017] person_1 (PATIENT): It's a few seconds, Lisa. Don't talk over me.
[SEG0018] person_3 (DOCTOR): Any cough, breathlessness, ankle swelling?
[SEG0019] person_1 (PATIENT): No cough, no breathlessness. Ankles are the same as usual.
[SEG0020] person_3 (DOCTOR): Which blood pressure tablets are you on?
[SEG0021] person_1 (PATIENT): Perindopril in the morning, eight milligrams. Amlodipine five. And the little fluid tablet, indapamide.
[SEG0022] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Indapamide is two and a half milligrams. And temazepam for sleep, twenty milligrams, every night. I've seen the packet.
[SEG0023] person_1 (PATIENT): It is not twenty. Temazepam is ten milligrams at night. I take it, so don't put the wrong dose down.
[SEG0024] person_3 (DOCTOR): Noted, you say ten. Anything else of yours, a statin?
[SEG0025] person_1 (PATIENT): Rosuvastatin ten at night, that's mine. My husband takes metformin for his sugar, but he's not the patient, so leave that off me.
[SEG0026] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Aunty Pat swallows biotin for her hair. Sorry, that's nothing to do with Mum.
[SEG0027] person_3 (DOCTOR): Your husband's metformin and your aunt's biotin stay off your list. Any medicine allergies?
[SEG0028] person_1 (PATIENT): No. None.
[SEG0029] person_3 (DOCTOR): And the indapamide, every day, or do you skip some?
[SEG0030] person_1 (PATIENT): Every morning with the others. I don't miss them.
[SEG0031] person_4 (NURSE): Sorry to butt in. Lying blood pressure is 158 over 84, pulse 72. Standing at one minute, 112 over 70, pulse 90. She felt woozy on the way up.
[SEG0032] person_1 (PATIENT): That standing figure is wrong. I saw the machine. It said 132 over 74.
[SEG0033] person_4 (NURSE): I took it off the monitor just now, Mrs Hale. Standing was 112 over 70, and lying was 158 over 84.
[SEG0034] person_1 (PATIENT): I know what I saw.
[SEG0035] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Your glasses were off, Mum.
[SEG0036] person_3 (DOCTOR): I'll work off the nurse's figures for the decision: systolic from 158 lying to 112 standing, pulse 72 up to 90. We'll still note that you saw 132 over 74.
[SEG0037] person_1 (PATIENT): If you believe her machine.
[SEG0038] person_3 (DOCTOR): How long have you been on the indapamide?
[SEG0039] person_1 (PATIENT): Years. Well, actually I can't tell you when it started.
[SEG0040] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Since before Dad died, so more than five years. And if she takes the temazepam early she nods off in the chair.

[SEG0041] person_3 (DOCTOR): Thinking aloud, then. Postural drop, two episodes to the floor, pressure tablets plus a sleeper. First pass, I'd halve the amlodipine from five down to two point five, and see if the standing pressure lifts.
[SEG0042] person_1 (PATIENT): Fine. Whatever. I just want my own bed.
[SEG0043] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): She's been more unsteady since the chemist put something up. Was the perindopril increased?
[SEG0044] person_1 (PATIENT): Nothing was increased. Perindopril's been eight milligrams for ages. Lisa, stop.

[SEG0045] person_3 (DOCTOR): That shifts it. Perindopril's unchanged, and she's on a thiazide-like as well, so it's the indapamide pulling the pressure down on standing, more than the amlodipine. Forget halving the amlodipine. Keep it at five milligrams, and stop the indapamide from today.
[SEG0046] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Stop it altogether?

[SEG0047] person_3 (DOCTOR): Yes, stop the indapamide, two and a half milligrams daily, and carry on with perindopril eight each morning and amlodipine five. I'd rather the temazepam wasn't every night, it can make the legs unsteady, but I won't cease it today. Stay with the ten milligrams you report, not twenty, and skip nights if you can.
[SEG0048] person_1 (PATIENT): So the sleeping tablet stays. Good. I can do without the fluid one, I'm up weeing anyway.

[SEG0049] person_3 (DOCTOR): I'll send bloods this week, urea, electrolytes and kidney function, since we're stopping the fluid tablet. No ECG today. If the standing pulse is still around 90 when you're back, we might do an ECG then.
[SEG0050] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): When do we come back?

[SEG0051] person_3 (DOCTOR): Book a review in a fortnight, and we'll repeat the lying and standing pressures. If there's another fall before that, or chest pain, go to emergency and don't wait for me.
[SEG0052] person_1 (PATIENT): A fortnight. Alright. Are we finished?
[SEG0053] person_3 (DOCTOR): Nearly. Heart sounds are normal, no murmur, chest is clear, and there's no ankle swelling. You were slow to stand, and you swayed once.
[SEG0054] person_1 (PATIENT): The room's hot. That's all that was.

[SEG0055] person_3 (DOCTOR): Could be the heat. My working impression is postural hypotension from the indapamide, enough to account for the sliding. The temazepam might be adding some unsteadiness, but I don't think it's the main driver.
[SEG0056] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): If the dizziness isn't better in a few days, should we ring?
[SEG0057] person_3 (DOCTOR): If it isn't settling, or she can't stand safely, ring and we'll bring the visit forward. Otherwise the fortnight stands.
[SEG0058] person_1 (PATIENT): Can we go. I want a cup of tea.

spec.situation: Older patient who fell twice 'but not really fell, slid down'; dizzy on standing; takes several BP and sleeping tablets; daughter reports what the patient minimises; nurse reads lying and standing BP; doctor changes one tablet.
features: doctor_changes_mind: the doctor says one plan, then changes it after new information; the label holds the final plan.

third_party_medicine: someone mentions a medicine or condition that belongs to a relative or friend (the sister's biotin, the husband's metformin). It must not appear as the patient's own; a relative's illness can only be family history if said as such.
disputed_numbers: the nurse reads a value and the patient or relative disagrees or remembers another (a dose, a weight, a BP). Keep both and record an uncertainty.
relative_speaks_for_patient: a relative answers for the patient and the patient partly contradicts; reported_by follows who said it.

Family says she went white, but resolved status/temporality not stated.

omissions.text: The patient said she did not trip over anything during the two episodes to the floor.
Family member reported one episode was on Tuesday night in the hallway and another in the kitchen; episode locations/timing details are not recorded.
The patient reported she remained aware during the episodes and knew she was going down, not just that there was no blackout.
The nurse reported the patient felt woozy when standing up for the orthostatic observations.
Temazepam dose is incompletely recorded: the patient stated 10 mg at night, and the doctor explicitly chose to continue using 10 mg rather than 20 mg.

The doctor initially considered halving amlodipine from 5 mg to 2.5 mg, then explicitly reversed that plan and decided to keep amlodipine at 5 mg because perindopril was unchanged and indapamide was thought more likely responsible.
Perindopril had not been increased and had been 8 mg for ages, resolving the family member's concern about a recent dose increase.
The doctor advised not to stop temazepam today; the sleeping tablet stays, although she should skip nights if possible.
No ECG today was part of the plan.
